messages.author: 146c5031f31e4913
messages.subject: is ddply the right tool?
parts:
Hi all, 

I have a data frame which is 0.8 Gb large (4+ million records), it has some unique owner ids and percentage ownership interests in various parcels of land. What I would like to do with it is to calculate a total percentage ownership interest for each owner and parcel combination--consolidate the records down to unique pairs of owners and land parcels. 

My thought is to use ddply (code below) but it takes 11 hours to run. Should I be thinking about this problem differently?

Thank you, 

Jake


consolidated_interests <-ddply(master[master$INTEREST_TYPE %in% title_codes, ], 
                                 .(LAND_AREA_NAME, LAND_AREA_CODE, OWNER_REFERENCE_NUMBER, TRACT_ID),
                                summarise, CONSOL_INTEREST = sum(OWNER_INTEREST), .progress = "text")

messages.author: e531efa2753b204e
messages.subject: Re: is ddply the right tool?
parts:
Forgot to forward to the list:

Using 'count' will be faster for a simple groupwise sum:

consolidated_interests <- count(

master[master$INTEREST_TYPE %in% title_codes, ],
    .(LAND_AREA_NAME, LAND_AREA_CODE, OWNER_REFERENCE_NUMBER, TRACT_ID),

wt_var="OWNER_INTEREST")

For more general group computations I've just submitted a patch to plyr (https://github.com/hadley/plyr/pull/172)  which should improve its performance for large numbers of groups. Can you try installing the patched version like so and see if it improves things?

install.packages(devtools)
library(devtools)
install_github("plyr", username="crowding", ref="fastrbind")

Peter

messages.author: 93fdeb4704061276
messages.subject: Re: is ddply the right tool?
parts:
If I had a calculation that required 11 hours, I'd start to consider moving the serious work out of R to a faster language, such as Fortran or C or C++.  Ordinarily, that has been a horrible challenge, but the package RcppEigen (or RcppArmadillo) offers a pretty convenient method do put the setup work in R and export the hard part to the fast language.

If you don't want to go that way, then look again at your R and use the R profiler to find out where your function is spending all of its time. Sometimes, it is wasting time in ways you never imagined.  Some of these facts I've learned from hard luck, where things I expected to be fast were slow (http://pj.freefaculty.org/guides/Rcourse/WorkingExamples/efficiency-stackListItems-01.R; http://pj.freefaculty.org/guides/Rcourse/WorkingExamples/efficiency-slowFunctionCalls-01.R;  http://pj.freefaculty.org/guides/Rcourse/WorkingExamples/efficiency-vectorize.R).

Remember that, in R, it is always fastest to "push" the calculations all the way out to R's C level, and a lot of the slowdown people notice is in the swapping of information between R and C.  That's why people always yell about "don't use for loops", because uses in R of the explicit index [] comeback to R, go back to C, every time.

I would not be surprised if a big part of  your slowdown is the calculation of the classification variable. You re-run this function, you are forcing the re-construction of the classification combination. This %in%  is SUPER SLOW.  Calculate that once, add its resutl to the data frame as a variable, then iterate on that.

I'm speaking from about 20 years of miscellaneous programming here, but I'm not a professional programmer.  So take my advice for what it is worth.

messages.author: fc772258f24953a6
messages.subject: Re: is ddply the right tool?
parts:
+1 for data.table. I've just started using it for heavy-lifting with
good speed results compared to plyr.

The syntax of plyr is much more user-friendly than data.table, and the
behavior of plyr is more predictable. Data.table is side-effect
heavy; I've found it really takes some careful documentation-reading
to master it and get maximal performance. In particular,
intellegently defining keys can make help.

As per Paul's comments about C/C++, data.table makes heavy use of
pass-by-reference, and so you get much less copying of objects in
memory when used correctly. I imagine that using Rcpp's cppFunction
paired with data.table's j= argument would work well. But your
example isn't very complicated.

## try this
## I can't verify syntax, but this should get you started...
##
require(data.table)
##
##turn into data.table, index
all.dt = data.table(master)
setkey(my.dt, INTEREST_TYPE, LAND_AREA_NAME, LAND_AREA_CODE,
OWNER_REFERENCE_NUMBER, TRACT_ID)
##
## subset. look at data.table docs for possibly more efficient subset options
sub.dt <- subset(all.dt, INTEREST_TYPE %in% title_codes)
##
## check that keys are preserved?
key(sub.dt)
##
##
consolidated_interests <- sub.dt[, j=data.table(CONSOL_INTEREST =
sum(.SD$OWNER_INTEREST)),
by=c('LAND_AREA_NAME', 'LAND_AREA_CODE', 'OWNER_REFERENCE_NUMBER',
'TRACT_ID')
]


Curious to hear your results!
Best,
Christian

This is a follow up post taking into account many of the suggestions all of you offered. Thank you all for your help, the feedback and the tests below helped me to learn some new stuff about certain packages and R in general. 

The first thing I did was to time how long it took plyr to run the task as I described it before. Test1 does the [ ] indexing within the ddply call and Test2 lets plyr operate on a pre-subsetted data.frame. (I shortened the data.frame to 20,000 rows for the test. At the reported speeds below it would have taken 13 hours for plyr to complete Test1 and Test2 would have taken 12 hours (PJ's [ ] suggestion).

Then, using Peter's advice, I use the simple count function, which sped things up drastically. Peter, I also tried the plyr version which had your patch from GitHub. After the restart of R, plyr gave me the same exact times as I report below. 

Dennis supplied working data.table code and I compare that to the new dplyr package installed from GitHub. Operating on the entire 4+ million rows, but doing the subset first, both dplyr and data.table reduced the hours of run time to mere seconds. With data.table's 2.68 seconds besting dplyr's 35.49.

I hope you find this informative. I posted my session info below also.

Jake
